copy_pick.why: Its blurb 'BRITAIN COLLARS IRAN BASE PLOTTERS' wears the tabloid directive best with one hard, cheeky verb, and its summary avoids yesterday's 'leaking/spreading' framing with a fresh 'branch office in the UK' joke and a sharp polar-vortex closer, while the others echo the 11-11 and 11-09 cards' war

doom.driver: An Iran-backed trio is accused of plotting attacks on a U.K. base hosting U.S. jets. Iran-backed operatives have been charged over nearly 20 attacks, including a plot on a U.K. base housing U.S. troops. Separately, a U.S. soldier is held in the U.K. on Russia spying claims.
doom.summary: Nearly 20 alleged attacks, one of them aimed at a British base full of American jets: the Iran war has apparently opened a branch office in the UK. Meanwhile the US Treasury Secretary now lives on a military base, Kushner and Witkoff are touring Moscow and Dublin, and Russia keeps switching off Ukraine's lights. The tech world is too busy watching Nvidia's boardroom soap opera to notice that the polar vortex just collapsed a month early.

factors.name: AI Capability
factors.detail: DeepMind verifying Signal's cryptography and AlphaGenome 2 decoding disease genetics point to AI quietly taking over serious scientific grunt work.

factors.name: Governance
factors.detail: The world's most important chip CEO may be fired over an alleged MSS spy affair, just as Congress moves to tighten China export controls.

factors.name: Geopolitics
factors.detail: Iran-backed plots on a UK base hosting US jets show a hot war spilling into allied territory while Ukraine and Gaza keep burning.

factors.name: Alignment
factors.detail: No rogue-model headlines today, just think pieces weighing open AI risks.

factors.name: Wild Card
factors.detail: A deadly ambush in Pakistan, Barcelona street clashes and an Indonesian resignation add noise but no global shockwave.

doom.dalle_prompt: Pixel art, 16-bit SNES style, no text, no antialiasing. An extreme close-up fills the whole frame: a creased broadsheet newspaper lies flat on a scarred oak table in a Suffolk village pub near RAF Lakenheath. The pub window at the top edge of the frame holds a reflected view of the flat Breckland horizon. A flint-walled church tower and a row of grass-mounded aircraft shelters sit under a sky of blood-red and furnace-orange cloud. A hellish orange glare rises from below the frame, from an unseen glowing bar heater at table level. It floods upward across the paper so every fold and ink block is plainly visible. Shadows fall in bruised violet and maroon. The newspaper's front page is the main subject. A huge halftone photo, built from chunky red and orange pixel dots, shows a gray F-15E Strike Eagle tail fin with twin vertical stabilizers rising from a hardened shelter behind a razor-wire fence. Beneath it sits a smaller halftone of three hooded figures in puffer jackets standing in a car park, each shown whole, with phone-glow faces. A third small inset shows a lone figure in a U.S. Army camouflage uniform with bowed head between two uniformed British officers, all fully visible. Thick black bars and blocks stand in for headline and body type, with no readable letters. At the right edge, a half-drunk pint of bitter glows amber and holds a tiny curved reflection of the burning sky. A beer mat printed with a Union Jack and Stars and Stripes pattern lies beside it, one corner scorched and curling. A cracked burner phone lies on the paper's corner with its screen glowing a sickly Iranian green. The mood is malevolent and nothing feels safe, and the whole scene stays bright and readable at phone size.

minor: The three hooded figures in the lower-left photo have dark, indistinct faces, with only small glowing phone lights. This matches the prompt and is fine at phone size.
The aircraft in the main photo is a dark halftone silhouette. The twin tail fins read clearly, but the fuselage and shelter blend into the fence and ground.
The Union Jack beer mat is partly cropped and its Stars and Stripes half is hard to make out. The scorched corner is subtle.
The phone screen shows a green blob with a dark shape, not a clearly cracked screen. It reads as a glowing phone.
The pint glass has a murky reflection, and the sky reflection is barely visible.
The headline and body-text blocks are plain black bars with no letters, so there is no garbled text.
The overall palette is very orange and dark, but the newspaper, glass and phone all stay readable.

dawn.driver: Australian teen missing in bush for six days rescued alive. The 17-year-old's mum has joked that he is "grounded for life" and "never leaving the house again".
dawn.blurb: SIX DAYS IN THE BUSH, THEN GROUNDED
dawn.summary: A 17-year-old who spent six days lost in the Australian bush is home, alive and in deep trouble with his mum, who says he is grounded for life and never leaving the house again. In southern Iraq the ancient marshes are coming back to life, and in Senegal young breakdancers are warming up for Africa's first-ever Olympic event. Off Florida, the record-setting SS United States has begun a new career as the world's largest artificial reef.

factors.name: Science
factors.detail: An independent re-analysis confirmed that the Event Horizon Telescope's famous black hole ring really is there, and general relativity holds up.

factors.name: Cooperation
factors.detail: Senegal is hosting the Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympic event ever held in Africa, and its breakdancers are ready to compete on home ground.

factors.name: Human Spirit
factors.detail: Searchers brought a teenager home alive after six days in the Australian bush, and his mother greeted the news with relief and a joke.

factors.name: Environment
factors.detail: Water is returning to southern Iraq's marshes, where one of the world's oldest ways of life is beginning to revive.

factors.name: Wild Card
factors.detail: At Children's Nebraska, window washers dressed as superheroes rappelled past patients' windows and made a hospital full of kids grin.

copy_pick.why: Candidate 3 recycles the superheroes-at-a-children's-hospital bit from 11-08, so Candidate 2 wins: its terse field-note headline wears today's form and its 'home, alive and in deep trouble with his mum' line lands the one human detail with the day's sharpest wit.

dawn.dalle_prompt: Pixel art, 16-bit SNES style, no text, no antialiasing. SILHOUETTE COMPOSITION in dense Victorian eucalypt forest east of Melbourne on Thursday morning, with the camera low in a ferny gully looking toward the sunrise. Towering gum trunks with peeling bark rise like dark columns, and a blazing amber-gold sun pours between them through soft drifting mist. The canopy of grey-green leaves is edged in glowing light, the forest floor is a carpet of bright soft-green ferns and damp leaf litter, and long shadows are lifting and thinning. In the middle distance a tall teenage boy stands upright and calm in a clearing, seen from behind as a pure black silhouette with no face, at the spot where he waited. Moving toward him through the mist are three rescuers in dark silhouette: a police officer with one arm outstretched, a second officer wiping their eyes, and a dog handler with a police dog straining happily ahead on its lead. At the right edge, a mother in silhouette runs into frame with her arms open, about to hold her son. A small helicopter hangs in the glowing sky between the trunks at upper left, its rotor wash stirring the mist. Warm amber light rims every figure, fern frond and strand of bark, and the palette is warm amber and soft green with clean morning clarity. The mood is a held breath released into relief.

minor: The helicopter's tail boom runs into a dark tree branch at upper left, so the two blur together a little.
The dog is small and lost in the mist beside the handler's legs, so it reads as a vague shape.
The rescuers are murky silhouettes. The one at far left is hard to read, and the 'wiping eyes' gesture is not clear.
The mother is cropped at the right edge. Her body is bulky and her rear leg and foot are a little awkward, but her arms and legs still connect to her body.
